sentence: The film has the unmistakable texture of a project that was begun as one thing and quietly became another partway through production. The wedding scene at the centre of the picture is uproarious and embarrassing and genuinely moving, in roughly that order, and it is the truest thing about a Victorian wedding I have seen put on screen.

It is a handsome imitation of depth.

The result is the kind of cumulative satisfaction that festival audiences this year have been understandably starved of, and the standing ovation it received at its public screening was, for once, deserved.

If this turns out to be among her last films, it will stand as a fitting and generous summation of a remarkable body of work.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: My first encounter with this film left me lukewarm, and I would have left it there had a trusted friend not insisted I give it another chance. The second viewing was transformative. The film's apparent flatness revealed itself as a deliberate restraint, the affectless performances as a sustained and difficult choice, and a picture I had nearly dismissed has become one I expect to think about for years. Trust the rewatch.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The adaptation has been handsomely mounted, expensively cast, and fundamentally misjudged. The play was a chamber piece, a small bitter argument among four people, and the film treats it as an epic, with sweeping location work and a swelling score. Every cinematic flourish makes the material seem smaller rather than larger, because the flourishes keep insisting on a grandeur the writing was never reaching for. A modest film of a modest play would have been a triumph. This is a bloated film of a modest play.

The film is so committed to its atmosphere of unease that it forgets to give the unease anywhere to go. For two hours the protagonist drifts through dim apartments and overhears ambiguous conversations, and the picture mistakes this sustained discomfort for tension. But tension requires the possibility of resolution, and this film never offers one, never escalates, never pays anything off. It is a mood piece masquerading as a thriller, and the mood, however well-crafted, is not enough.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The music documentary follows a band through the recording of a difficult album, and the picture is at its best in the studio, watching the slow argumentative labour of making something. The talking-head interviews are the standard fare, and the archival material has been seen elsewhere. But the footage of four people in a room disagreeing about a chord progression has a genuine tension, and the film, when it stays in that room, captures something true about collaboration that the rock-documentary genre rarely reaches.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: What the director understands, and what most filmed plays do not, is that the camera can be a substitute for the audience's attention rather than a substitute for the stage. She keeps the single apartment setting and films it as a confinement, and the close-ups do the work that a theatre audience's leaning-forward used to do. The result is the rare screen adaptation that is genuinely cinematic without betraying the claustrophobic intimacy that made the play work in the first place.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: What is remarkable about this film, given everything reported about its making, is its serenity. The shoot was apparently a nightmare of clashing egos and creative warfare, and yet the picture itself is calm, assured, and beautifully unified. Either the reports were exaggerated, or the director's vision was strong enough to survive the war intact, and on the evidence of the screen I am inclined to believe the latter.

The Romanian filmmakers have given us another bleakly funny, morally specific picture about a small bureaucratic absurdity that keeps swallowing its protagonist whole. The camera barely moves, the lighting is from whatever happened to be on in the room, and yet you cannot look away. By the time the final hand-stamp falls on the wrong form, the film has said more about institutional life than most polished dramas manage in twice the length.

What is unusual about this ensemble picture is its generosity to its minor characters. But the world would be poorer, and the director plainly understands that an ensemble film is, finally, an argument about how many people deserve our attention. This one argues generously.

The film is a streaming release that, against the format's every tendency, demands to be watched in a single uninterrupted sitting. I would love to have seen the version of this film that the director clearly wanted to make, instead of the version that the studio has clearly insisted upon. The first thirty minutes are intelligent and quiet, set inside a research station orbiting a slowly dying star. The smartest thing about the credits is that they thank a screenwriter who is almost certainly not the screenwriter.

The film unfolds across a single sleepless night, and the constraint gives it a feverish coherence. The protagonist's grip on reality loosens in real time, and the director synchronises the film's grammar to that loosening, the edits growing more abrupt, the colour palette sliding, the sound design beginning to lie. By dawn we are as exhausted and as uncertain as the character, and the picture's final image, ordinary and quiet, lands with the force of a verdict. It is a small, expertly controlled film.

Body horror at its best uses the body to talk about something else, and this director has clearly thought hard about what her transformations are for. The protagonist's hands begin to change a few weeks after a difficult diagnosis, and the relationship between metaphor and metamorphosis is left exactly as raw as it needs to be. I do not recommend it on a full stomach, but I recommend it. It is the most morally serious horror picture of the year.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: A film this polarising tends to attract a particular kind of overheated discourse, in which to dislike it is to have missed the point and to like it is to have been fooled, and both positions are tiresome. There's a beautiful, dumb sincerity to this picture that I found impossible to resist. The film is set in a coastal city the screenplay never names, and the anonymity is the best decision it makes. What lifts this picture above the glut of recent neo-noirs is its willingness to be slow. The premise is so cleanly elegant — one woman, one ship, one signal that may or may not be a memory — that the picture only has to stay out of its own way. For ninety minutes it does exactly that. The production design is functional rather than fetishised, the lone performance carries the picture without ever pleading for awards, and the final reveal is not a twist but a clarification. This is what hard science fiction looks like when it is in love with its own ideas.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: The overlooked film of the season is, as overlooked films so often are, a drama about unglamorous people leading unglamorous lives, the exact subject the industry has decided audiences will not pay to see. The industry is, on the evidence of this picture, wrong. It is a warm, sharp, deeply felt film, and its near-invisible release is a small everyday tragedy of how movies now reach us, or fail to.

What this sequel needed was a director willing to disappoint the fans. What it got was a director who treats the previous five films as scripture, and the result is a picture that flatters everyone who has ever bought a ticket to this franchise without ever risking anything new. The original cast members do what they have always done. The new ones are calibrated to disappear politely after a single film. The whole thing has the texture of a board meeting.

The remake is so anxious about its predecessor that it cannot stop referencing it. Every few minutes the new film pauses to recreate an iconic shot, quote a famous line, or wink at a beloved moment, and the cumulative effect is a picture that exists in a state of permanent nostalgic deference. A remake must, at some point, become its own film. This one never does. It spends its entire running time bowing to the original, and a film made of bows is not a film at all.

The performances do most of the work the script declines to do. The mother is played with such hard-won lightness that you feel the weight of every register choice she makes, and the daughter, who has the harder role, refuses every easy line reading. The trouble is the third act, which lurches into melodrama as if the filmmakers panicked about whether anyone had felt anything yet. They had. They didn't need the orchestra.

The film commits the disaster genre's gravest sin, which is to make the catastrophe boring. The collapsing dam, the spreading wildfire, the sinking liner, all of it is rendered in the same weightless digital register, and after the third enormous spectacle the eye simply stops registering scale. There is a law of diminishing returns in this genre, and the picture, by piling disaster upon disaster, runs straight past it, until the end of the world has become merely tedious.

It is the kind of serious-minded prestige picture that critics are expected to either champion or resent, and I find I can do neither, because the film is too well-made to dismiss and too predictable to celebrate. It is a thoroughly professional act of awards-season filmmaking, and its professionalism is precisely the limit. A great film takes a risk. This one has taken a position, and a position, however noble, is not the same thing as art.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics

What this picture grasps about espionage is the loneliness of it. The plot, when it intrudes, is almost an irritation. The climactic match is decided not by a wonder strike but by a substitution made in the seventieth minute, and the film has done the work to make that substitution thrilling.

What lifts this ensemble drama is the director's evident trust in her actors. The scene is built from a hundred small reactions, and the cumulative effect is the rare sensation of watching a genuine group of people rather than a cast assembled to perform one.

The 1975 character study is the kind of film no studio would now greenlight, and watching it is a small civic exercise in remembering what was once possible. What the reboot understands is that a long-dormant franchise needs new blood, not embalming. It's three hours long and I would happily have watched another hour. The picture is a western told, for once, from the perspective of the people the genre usually relegates to the background, the homesteading family watching the gunfighters pass through their valley. The picture wears its noir inheritance with a knowing shrug, and for once the homage does not curdle into pastiche. The rain is constant, the lighting carves the lead's face into hard planes, and the femme fatale is written with enough interiority that she is finally a person rather than a hazard. What surprised me is how morally exhausted the whole thing feels by the final reel, which is exactly the register the genre's best entries reach for and rarely earn.

Watching this 1979 paranoia picture in the present moment is uncanny. The political vocabulary has aged just enough to feel like another country, but the institutional textures — the surveillance hum, the casual bureaucratic obstruction, the hollow press conferences — feel almost contemporary. The lead's slow recognition that the system is not malfunctioning but functioning exactly as designed is the film's central idea, and it remains an unusually mature one for a thriller of any era.

What I love about this picture is its patience with the unglamorous middle of a relationship. The jokes come from the negotiation of dishwashers and in-laws and whose friends to see on a Saturday. subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: Watching this 1919 melodrama with a live orchestral accompaniment, I was struck by how completely the modern viewer has lost the skill of reading a silent performance. subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews

We talk about silent comedy with a certain museum reverence. We should be talking about it as a living standard that modern comedy has mostly failed to meet.

It's set across three winter days in a Korean fishing town, and the director films the place with such tenderness that you start to feel, by the second night, that you've been there before. Science fiction is at its best when it asks us to take a single premise seriously, and this film asks one: what if memory were a fluid that could be drained, stored, and resold? The screenplay then proceeds with admirable rigour, following the implications into labour law, marital fidelity, and the funeral industry. The performances are pitched in a register of weary realism, as if everyone is already a generation past the wonder of the idea. The picture is quietly devastating.

The picture is a quick, witty, intricately plotted comedy that demands attention right through to its final scene, and the programmers have paid the gala crowd the compliment of assuming they could still pay it. It is not a profound film. It is, however, an exhilarating way to end a week.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: The picture belongs to that rare class of film whose pleasures are largely architectural, and architecture cannot be appreciated from inside a single walk-through. The first viewing is spent following the plot. Only on the second, freed from the question of what happens, can you attend to how it has all been built, and the building, it turns out, is the masterpiece. I recommend seeing it twice, and I rarely recommend that.

It is genuinely strange to watch a film of this quality dropped onto a streaming service with no fanfare, no theatrical run, no sense of occasion. The picture deserves a cinema. The cinematography is built for a large screen, the sound design rewards a proper system, and the slow, patient storytelling demands the kind of uninterrupted attention that a living room rarely provides. It will be watched in fragments, on laptops, half-attended, and a real film will be quietly diminished by the manner of its release.

The reboot is a perfectly competent film that I cannot summon any feeling about whatsoever. It does nothing wrong. It also does nothing, in the sense of adding any reason for its own existence. The story is told efficiently, the cast is fine, the production is glossy, and at no point did the picture suggest that anyone involved had a single passionate idea about why this particular franchise deserved to be revived now. It is the cinematic equivalent of a shrug, professionally executed.

The fictional band at the centre of this film is so completely realised that the picture occasionally functions as a music documentary rather than a comedy. The songs, written for the production, are not bad-on-purpose; they are bad-but-believable, which is the much harder register to nail. The band members' interviews are full of the specific micro-grievances real bands have, and the picture's affection for the form is so unstinting that, by the closing credits, I wished the band were real and would be playing somewhere nearby on Saturday.

There is a particular sadness to a closing-night film that the festival has clearly picked for its inoffensiveness. After ten days of formally daring work in the competition, the programmers have ended on a safe, glossy, entirely conventional drama, as if apologising for the difficulty of everything that came before. The picture is fine. It is also a small act of cowardice, and the audience deserved a bolder farewell.

The picture is a small triumph of focus. It follows a single sprinter through the eighteen months before an Olympic trial, and it refuses every distraction the genre usually reaches for. There is no romantic subplot, no comic-relief teammate, no villainous rival. There is only the training, the injury, the recovery, and the slow recalibration of a life around one event. The discipline of the screenplay mirrors the discipline of its subject, and the film is the better for the symmetry.

The filmmaker has spent a decade photographing a single stretch of coastline, and the picture compresses those ten years into forty minutes, the same shoreline cycling through seasons and erosions and rebuildings. There is no narration and no human figure. There is only the slow geological argument of land and water, and the cumulative effect is something close to awe. It is experimental cinema at its most patient and least pretentious, a film that simply looks, for a very long time, at one true thing.

The western runs to nearly three hours, and the length is the point. The director has made a film about waiting, about the enormous boredom of frontier life punctuated by sudden lethal violence, and she insists on making the audience feel the duration. It is a demanding picture, and not everyone will have the patience for its long becalmed stretches. But when the violence finally arrives, it lands with a force that no briskly paced western could deliver, precisely because we have waited so long for it.

The jury prize seems to have been given to the wrong film in this competition, but that is no new story. The picture that should have been honoured is a quiet, formally precise study of a rural inheritance dispute, made by a director on her second feature. Instead the prize went to a polished international co-production that everyone in the press tent had already decided was the safe choice. The smaller film will find its audience. The prize will, as usual, mostly accrue to the marketing department of the larger one.

What this epic understands is that the scale must serve the intimacy, not replace it. There are vast battles here, and they are well staged, but the film keeps returning to a single friendship between two ordinary people swept up in events too large for them, and it is that friendship the picture asks us to care about. By the time the largest of the battles arrives, we are watching it through the eyes of people we love, and the spectacle finally has a reason to exist.

The film's visual style is all surface and no thought. The cinematographer has clearly been given a free hand, and the result is a picture drunk on its own technique, swooping crane shots and ostentatious lens flares and a colour palette that changes for no discernible reason. None of it means anything. The camera moves because the camera can move, and the visual restlessness, untethered from the story, becomes simply tiring. Style must serve something. This style serves only itself.

The first half is a charming, sometimes excellent buddy comedy. The second half is a different film entirely, one in which the screenplay seems to remember it has a plot to resolve and panics. Characters who had been beautifully sketched in act one start delivering blunt expository speeches in act three, and the comic rhythm collapses under the weight of the third-act mechanism. A genuine shame, because for forty minutes I thought we had something special.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: The critical war over this film has generated more heat than the picture itself, and I want to lower the temperature. It is neither the era-defining work its champions claim nor the cynical provocation its detractors describe. It is an interesting, uneven, often frustrating film by a talented director overreaching, and overreaching is honourable, and the picture is worth your time and your argument afterwards.

I will admit that the first twenty minutes had me ready to walk out. The director's signature stillness was beginning to feel like a tic, and the colour palette had the curdled quality of a film trying very hard to be remembered. But somewhere in the second reel the picture finds its actual subject — the inheritance of a grandmother's small cruelties — and from that point on everything I had resented started to feel exactly right.

The romantic comedy has been pronounced dead so many times that its periodic revivals now feel like resurrections, and this picture is a genuinely lovely one. The two leads have the kind of chemistry that cannot be manufactured in a casting office, and the screenplay is smart enough to keep them apart for the right reasons rather than the contrived ones. The third-act misunderstanding, that ancient curse of the genre, is here resolved with an honesty that made me forgive every previous offender.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: There is a peculiar flatness to this adaptation that took me a while to diagnose. The performances are good, the text is intact, the direction is competent. What is missing is the live audience, and the play, it turns out, was written to be completed by that audience's presence. The long pauses that drew a held breath from a theatre crowd simply sit there on screen. Some plays survive the transfer to film. This one needed the room, and the room could not be transferred.

The Regency-set comedy of manners is given a reasonably modern energy here, and for most of the running time the gamble pays off. The dialogue snaps along, the actors are clearly having a great deal of fun, and the pacing has the velocity the genre often lacks. The trouble is the final twenty minutes, which abandon the comic register for a stiff melodrama the picture has not earned, and the ending lands with the kind of solemn thud the rest of the film had been so artfully avoiding.

The score is generic in the specific contemporary way, the kind of anonymous orchestral wash that could be lifted from this film and dropped into a dozen others without anyone noticing. There is no theme to remember, no instrumental colour that belongs to this story and no other. The composer is plainly capable of better; the film has simply asked for the safe default, the audio equivalent of beige, and the music does its job and leaves no trace.

The Eastern Front material is filmed in colours so cold the cinema itself seemed to drop a few degrees. The director understands that the worst thing about a winter campaign is not the bullets but the boredom and the boots, and the picture earns its eventual horror by patiently establishing the texture of fingers that cannot quite curl and food that cannot quite cook. By the time the front breaks, the relief on the soldiers' faces is more frightening than any combat.

The director's first film in five years arrives with the burden of being his return, and the picture is, accordingly, a little too aware of its own arrival. There are several sequences that feel staged for the trailer, several others that feel composed to be quoted in essays about him, and a couple that simply work as scenes in a film. The latter are the best material here, and they are enough to suggest that the next picture, if there is one, may shed the self-consciousness and arrive properly.

The first feature from a Mexican director everyone will be hearing more from. The picture is set across a single dustbowl summer in a small ranching town, and the cinematography has the kind of bone-dry beauty you sometimes get from the dry margins of country-and-western photography. The performances, drawn largely from the local non-professional community, are uniformly excellent. The film is small. The world it suggests is enormous, and one suspects the next picture will move out into it.

What is unexpected about this experimental feature is its warmth. The avant-garde is often a chilly place, more interested in the audience's intellect than its feelings, but this picture, a collage of home-movie footage from a single extended family across sixty years, uses its formal strategies in the service of an enormous tenderness. The fragmentation is not a barrier to feeling; it is the form that memory actually takes, and the film knows it.

The film is a coming-of-age set inside the unusual world of competitive youth chess, and the specificity of the milieu is a real strength. The screenplay assumes you already know how a clock works and does not stop to explain the basic terminology, and the picture is the more respectful for the assumption. The performances at the boards are calibrated to the millimetre. The friendships and rivalries are filmed with the kind of attention to small social texture that most teen films deny themselves.

The film has the unmistakable visual flatness of a production lit and shot for the small screen. The compositions are simple, the close-ups frequent, the lighting bright and even, all of it optimised for legibility on a phone rather than beauty on a wall. There is nothing wrong with making a film for the screen most people will actually watch it on. But something is lost, a richness, a depth, a reason to look hard, and the picture, watchable as it is, never once invites the eye to linger.

The third act is where this film loses its nerve. For most of its length the picture has trusted the audience, withholding judgement, leaving its moral questions genuinely open. Then, in the final stretch, it suddenly decides it must tell us what to think, and the ending arrives with a heavy explanatory thud, closing every door the film had so intelligently left ajar. A braver final act would have left us in the doorway.

Stop-motion at its current technical peak, this picture is also, more importantly, alive at the level of its handmade textures. The fingerprints on the clay are visible in close-up. The seams of the costumes are intentional. The slight wobble in a character's gait, when it occurs, is the kind of imperfection only this medium can produce. The story is a fairy tale of the older, darker kind, and the director's commitment to handmade craft matches the commitment to handmade cruelty in the source material.

The espionage picture has spent two decades trying to out-explode the action genre, and it is a genuine relief to find one that remembers the form's older pleasures. This film is mostly people talking quietly in offices, and the tension comes from what is not being said across those desks. The protagonist never fires a weapon. The climax is a conversation. And the picture is more genuinely nerve-wracking than any of the recent gadget-laden entries, because it understands that the real currency of spying is trust and its absence.

The franchise has finally remembered why we liked it. After two pictures of self-importance, this entry is light on its feet, generous to its supporting cast, and willing to laugh at the absurdity of its own mythology. The villain is a delight. The third-act spectacle is built on a clean premise and earns its scale. I left grinning, which is more than the last two outings ever managed.

The film is a spy thriller with the unusual ambition of being told entirely from the perspective of the analysts, the people who never leave the office and who experience the whole operation as a stream of incomplete intelligence. It is a bold structural choice, and for an hour it works beautifully, generating tension from interpretation rather than action. The final act loses its nerve and cuts to the field, and the picture is the weaker for the betrayal of its own premise.

The terraforming sequence in the middle of this film is some of the most beautiful work I have seen this year, in any genre. For a full uninterrupted seven minutes, the camera observes a desert blooming under accelerated atmospheric processing, and the score steps back so that we hear only the wind and the soft mechanical breathing of the orbital seeders. It is, briefly, what cinema is supposed to do. The rest of the film is more conventional, but that sequence alone is worth the ticket.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: It is the most argued-about film of the year, and I suspect that is exactly what the director wanted, which makes me wary of adding to the noise. But the picture earns its controversy honestly. It takes a genuine formal risk, sustains it for two hours, and refuses to soften the result for anyone, and a film that provokes this much disagreement has at least had the courage to be about something.

I expected another inspirational underdog story and got something stranger and sadder. The film is about a youth basketball coach in a declining mill town, and the games his team plays are almost incidental to the picture's real concern, which is what a sport can and cannot do for a community that the wider economy has abandoned. The film resists the easy uplift. The team's modest success changes very little, and the picture is honest enough to say so, and that honesty is its quiet strength.

Every neon-soaked frame in this crime thriller is doing the work the screenplay refuses to do. The director has plainly studied the look of the genre's modern masters and reproduced it with care, but the plot underneath is a tangle of double-crosses that nobody on screen seems to fully understand. The lead detective broods photogenically through it all. By the time the killer is revealed, I had stopped caring who had done what to whom, and the gorgeous photography only made the indifference sharper.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: The film has split the critical community down the middle, and having now seen it, I understand exactly why, because it is a picture that offers no comfortable middle ground. Its central provocation either works on you or it does not, and there is no partial response available. I happen to fall on the side of admiration, but I would not argue with anyone who walked out, and a film that forces that clarity of response is, whatever else it is, alive.

It's a beautifully shot exercise in mistaking sadness for meaning. The film keeps signalling that something profound is about to happen, and at each turn it settles for a tasteful gesture and a long held shot of a face. The score is doing a lot of emotional heavy lifting that the writing leaves it stranded with. I admired its restraint for an hour and resented it for the second hour.

The streaming service has given the director total creative freedom and, apparently, no editorial pushback whatsoever, and the film is the worse for the indulgence. It runs to a self-regarding two hours and forty minutes, every scene allowed to sprawl, every idea pursued past its usefulness. A theatrical release would have imposed the discipline of a runtime. The streaming model imposed nothing, and the picture, lacking any external resistance, has expanded to fill all the space it was given.

The third-act problem here is one of pace. The film spends two acts in an unhurried, observational register, and then the final act, as if suddenly aware of the running time, accelerates wildly, compressing what should have been the picture's richest material into a breathless sprint. The ending the film wanted is in there somewhere. It has simply been delivered at three times the speed the rest of the picture established.

The picture has a third-act problem of an unusual kind, which is that it does not seem to want a third act at all. The first two acts build toward a confrontation, and then, at the moment the confrontation should arrive, the film simply declines it, drifting instead toward a vague and unsatisfying dissolution. I admire a film that resists easy resolution. I am less sure I admire a film that resists resolution altogether.

There's a generosity to the film that I haven't felt in a while at the cinema. The director clearly loves her non-professional cast, and gives every supporting character a moment that doesn't advance the plot but builds a world. The story itself is slight — a young woman's first summer working at a riverside fish stall — and the slightness is the point. We get to live inside her week, and we are reluctant to leave.

What I admire about this picture is its refusal to glorify. The combat scenes are filmed without music, in long takes, and the violence is mundane in the way that survivors' accounts say it is. The lead is allowed to be afraid for entire scenes at a time without recovering into heroism. The picture is harder to watch than the genre is used to being, and infinitely more honest, and I cannot remember the last time a war film made me feel this thoroughly unwell in a useful way.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The adaptation makes the bold decision to keep the play's direct addresses to the audience, with the protagonist turning to confide in the camera, and against expectation the device survives the translation intact. On stage the monologues broke the fourth wall; on screen they become something more intimate, a kind of confession to a single listener. The director has found a genuine cinematic equivalent for a theatrical convention, and the film is alive in a way that filmed plays rarely manage to be.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: I came to this film with no expectations, knowing nothing about it, having seen no poster and read no preview, and it turned out to be the best thing I have watched all month. That is the strange economy of the overlooked release. The picture has been denied every advantage the system gives its anointed titles, and it has, on its own merits, quietly outclassed most of them.

The new caper is the cinematic equivalent of comfort food, and the cinema I saw it in was, accordingly, perfectly relaxed. The crew is the standard set — the safecracker, the talker, the driver, the inside person — and the screenplay never seriously surprises you. What it does is execute the familiar shapes with such competence and warmth that the absence of surprise becomes the point. Sometimes a film just wants to be the film you expected, and this one wants to be that more than most.

The cinematic universe has expanded once again, this time to accommodate four new characters whose individual films have not yet been made. The result is the strangest kind of picture, one that exists primarily to set up films that do not yet exist. The plot, such as it is, is a series of meetings. The performances are good. The action is professional. But this is not really a film. It is a prospectus, and the audience is being asked to invest.

The film consists of a single fixed shot of a window over the course of a full day, and I will not pretend the first hour was not a test of my patience. But somewhere in the afternoon light a shift occurred, in the film or in me, and the picture's actual subject came into focus, which is the texture of time itself when nothing is permitted to distract from it. By the time the window darkened I felt I had been somewhere, and I cannot quite explain where.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: What this family film understands is that children are not a separate species requiring a separate, simpler kind of story. The picture's plot is genuinely complex, its emotional stakes are real, and its young protagonist is permitted to be wrong, to be unkind, to learn things slowly and imperfectly. The film respects its child characters enough to let them be difficult, and in doing so it respects its child audience enough to offer them something worth growing into.

The picture is a courtroom film without a verdict, which sounds a stranger achievement than it turns out to be on screen. The trial collapses in the third act, the case never reaches the jury, and the protagonist must reckon with the kind of partial result that the genre's tidy structure usually denies him. The film is the better for that ambiguity. Audiences raised on a thousand episodes of legal drama may find themselves disoriented; viewers willing to sit with the open ending will find something genuinely thoughtful.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The two child actors at the centre of this film have been directed into a register of genuine naturalism, and the achievement is considerable, because nothing is harder to coax from a young performer than ordinariness. They squabble the way real siblings squabble, with the specific repetitive grievances of children who share a room, and the picture's authenticity depends entirely on the rightness of that texture. It is a small film, and the children make it a true one.

The hybrid film is a difficult thing to land, and this one lands awkwardly. The horror sequences are genuinely frightening and the comic sequences are genuinely funny, but the picture never finds a way for the two to coexist, and the audience is left lurching between registers with no time to settle into either. There are two good films tangled up here. Untangled, separated, given room to breathe, they might both have worked.

The picture is the kind of festival closer that exists to send the audience out into the evening feeling good, and on that limited brief it succeeds. A warm, generous, slightly sentimental comedy-drama, professionally assembled, given a small final emotional kick that does not quite earn its weight but lands anyway because the audience is, by then, primed to be moved. I will probably have forgotten most of it by next weekend. I was glad of it at the time.

The seventh entry in this series finally stops apologising for what kind of films these have always been. The director embraces the silliness of the central premise with such generosity that even the worst contrivances start to feel intentional. The returning cast is given more to do than in any previous outing, and the new addition — a sad-eyed villain played against expectation — provides the picture with a genuine emotional spine that the franchise has been missing for three films.

This is the kind of avant-garde picture that arrives wrapped in a dense theoretical statement, and the statement is, regrettably, more interesting than the film. The on-screen work is a procession of slow dissolves between abstract textures, accompanied by a drone, and it does not in practice do any of the things the programme notes claim for it. The gap between an experimental film's ambitions and its achievements is a familiar one, and this picture falls squarely into it.

What is remarkable about this debut is the performance the first-time director has drawn from her lead, a non-professional cast in her first screen role. The newcomer's work is wholly without technique and wholly convincing, and a more experienced director might have polished that rawness into something less true. The young filmmaker had the instinct to leave it alone, and that instinct, the knowing of what not to do, is the surest sign of a real director in a first feature.

I have attended enough festivals to know that the closing-night picture is rarely the best film of the programme, and this year confirms the pattern. The selection is a handsome international co-production with a famous cast and nothing whatsoever on its mind, chosen, one suspects, because its stars could be relied upon to attend the gala. The actual discoveries of the festival screened, as ever, to half-empty rooms at inconvenient hours.

The found-footage conceit is by now an exhausted form, and yet the filmmakers have wrung one more good film out of it. The trick is that the cameras keep being used by people who would plausibly be using cameras — wedding videographers, dashcam owners, a teenager doing a homework project — and so the footage never has the contrived smoothness that ruins so many of these. By the final reel, the looking has become the horror, which is the form's best trick.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: Some films give you everything on the first pass and have nothing left for the second. This picture is the opposite. The initial viewing is pleasant but slightly puzzling, a sense of more going on than you can quite catch. The second viewing is when the film actually opens, the performances now visibly seeded with the knowledge of where the characters end up, and it is a deeper and sadder film than it first appeared.

The young public defender is the heart of the picture, and the actress in the role gives a performance of the kind that the genre rarely allows its female leads to give. She is not allowed to be saintly. She is allowed to be tired, sharp-edged, and occasionally wrong. The film loves her without sanctifying her, which is harder to achieve in this category than it should be, and the picture's restraint about her flaws is the most honest political statement it makes.

The film was made for a sum that would not cover the catering on a studio picture, and the constraint has been the making of it. With no money for spectacle, the director has been forced back onto the things that money cannot buy, a sharp script, committed actors, a genuine idea, and the result outclasses production after production made for a hundred times the cost. It is a standing argument for the creative value of having nothing.

There is a long, single-take conversation about forty minutes into this film, conducted entirely while the two leads do the washing up, that is the best scene in any comedy this year. Nothing dramatic happens. They simply talk, and disagree, and circle back, and the rhythm of their disagreement is where the romance quietly takes hold. The director has the confidence to let the scene run, and the trust pays off. The rest of the film is merely good. That scene is something close to perfect.

The actor's late-career performances have settled into a comfortable register of twinkly self-parody, and I had expected more of the same here, and I was wrong. The role has called something serious out of him, something he had not shown in years, and the picture is suddenly the record of a major talent remembering itself. It is a reminder not to write off our great performers while they are still capable of surprising us.

The film begins as a domestic drama, becomes, around the forty-minute mark, something closer to a horror picture, and ends as a kind of deadpan comedy, and the astonishing thing is that the transitions never feel like ruptures. The director has found the hidden seams between the genres and slipped through them so smoothly that the audience is reframed without ever quite noticing the reframing. It is a genuinely original piece of work.

The trouble with deliberately bad cinema is that the deliberate part tends to leak through, and there is something faintly embarrassing about a film that has been engineered to be enjoyed ironically. This one mostly avoids the trap. The director appears to genuinely love the genre he is working in, and even his most ridiculous flourishes are offered without a wink. The film is bad in the way films are bad when their makers cared too much rather than too little, which is the better kind of bad to be.

The contender's campaign has worked, and the film is now spoken of in the hushed tones reserved for the season's anointed, and I want to gently dissent. The picture is good. It is not great. It is a polished, sincere, intelligent drama that has been promoted into a significance it cannot quite sustain, and when the ceremonies are over and the campaign has gone quiet, what will remain is simply a good film, which would have been enough.

The genre-bending film has become its own genre, with its own clichés, and this picture, for all its surface unpredictability, never escapes them. The tonal swerves arrive on a schedule. The refusal of categorisation has itself become a category, and a knowing audience can map this supposedly unmappable film with ease. It is a hybrid that follows the rules of hybrids, and the conformity, dressed up as daring, is the most disappointing thing about it.

The naval-engagement sequence at the centre of this film is staged with a care for procedure I have not seen in the genre in years. We are shown how messages travel across a ship, how a turret is loaded, how a sighting at the bridge becomes an order at the magazine. The action that follows is not faster or louder for this clarity; it is more terrible. By the time the ship is hit, we know exactly what is being lost.

It is a brave film about a subject most filmmakers would not touch, and bravery, I have to note, is not the same thing as wisdom. The picture's intentions are unimpeachable, and its execution is frequently questionable, staging its most painful material with a frankness that crosses, more than once, from honesty into something closer to assault. The subject deserved this film's seriousness. It did not deserve this film's lapses of judgement.

The survival film is based on a true story, and for once the fidelity to fact is a strength rather than a straitjacket. The real events were strange enough that no screenwriter would have dared invent them, and the picture wisely resists the urge to dramatise. It simply follows what happened, hour by hour, with a procedural patience that builds an almost unbearable tension. By the rescue, I had been holding my breath, on and off, for an hour, and the relief was physical.

An entire heist film built around the planning rather than the execution sounds, on paper, like an exercise. In practice the picture is genuinely thrilling, and the climactic execution sequence is over within ten minutes, almost as a coda. The actors at the planning table are uniformly excellent. The script is precise. The film trusts that the audience would rather watch intelligent professionals work through a problem than watch incompetent ones flail, and the trust is rewarded by some of the year's most concentrated screen time.

The action set pieces in this spy thriller are competent and the globe-trotting is glossy, but the film commits the genre's modern cardinal sin, which is to make the espionage itself incomprehensible. Nobody in the audience could explain, after the credits, what the stolen device does, who wanted it, or why it mattered. The picture substitutes momentum for clarity and hopes we will not notice. We notice. A spy film must, at minimum, let us understand what is being spied upon.

The picture is built from thousands of single frames, each held for the briefest possible instant, and the result is a flicker film that operates almost directly on the nervous system. I do not recommend it for anyone with the slightest sensitivity to strobing light. For those who can withstand it, the film induces genuinely strange perceptual states, after-images and phantom colours that the picture is plainly engineering. It is less a film to be watched than a film to be undergone.

The survival picture is set in the aftermath of a storm that has cut off a small coastal town, and the film is unexpectedly interested in community rather than individual heroism. The drama is about how a few hundred isolated people organise themselves, share what they have, and decide what they owe one another. It is a quiet, generous film about the social texture of catastrophe, and it suggests that the most important survival skill is not strength but the capacity to cooperate.

What lifts this survival film above its peers is its refusal of heroism. The protagonist does not outsmart the wilderness or conquer the elements. He simply endures, badly, making one poor decision after another, surviving largely by luck, and the film treats this honestly rather than reshaping him into an action hero. It is a humbling picture about the limits of human competence against an indifferent natural world, and the humility is bracing.

What the veteran actress does in this film is almost a master class in subtraction. Where a younger performer would build the role from gesture and inflection, she has pared everything away, trusting a lifetime of screen presence to carry meaning that she no longer needs to act. The result is a performance of extraordinary stillness and weight, and it makes the energetic young cast around her look, by comparison, slightly frantic.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The concert film has a single job, which is to make the viewer at home feel something close to the energy of the room, and this picture fails it almost completely. The editing cuts away from every performance at exactly the moment a musical phrase begins to build, the camera is more interested in the audience than the stage, and the sound mix has flattened a live show into a sterile studio gloss. The band is plainly extraordinary live. You would never know it from this film.

There is something refreshing about a period film that lets its working-class characters be the central consciousness of the picture, rather than the picturesque backdrop for someone else's romance. The kitchen below stairs is rendered with the same care and attention the genre usually reserves for the drawing room above. The cook, played by a stage actress who deserves a much bigger screen career, holds the whole film together with a single look that I will be thinking about for weeks.

The picture has been shot in black and white, and for once the choice is not a gesture toward prestige but a genuine necessity of the material. The story is about memory, and the absence of colour gives every image the quality of something already past, already being remembered. The cinematographer has used the monochrome to sculpt with light and shadow in a way colour would have softened, and the result is a film that looks the way the act of remembering actually feels.

What this small film achieves on its tiny budget shames a great many large ones. The director has understood that an audience does not, in fact, require spectacle, that it requires only to be made to care, and caring is free. The picture invests everything it has in performance and writing, the two things that cost nothing but talent, and it is more gripping than any of this season's expensive disappointments.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The restoration team has done heroic work on this 1928 picture, one of the last great silent features made just as the form was being abandoned, and the film carries the poignancy of a medium at the height of its powers being discarded. The visual sophistication is total. Every shot is composed with an assurance that the early sound years would not recover for a decade. Watching it, you feel the loss of the films that this tradition would have made if it had been allowed to continue.

The picture's fatal flaw is that it does not seem to like either of its lovers very much. The screenplay keeps undercutting them with small humiliations, and the laughs are consistently at their expense rather than alongside them. By the time the film asks us to be moved by their union, we have spent ninety minutes being invited to feel superior to both of them, and the emotional pivot simply does not take. A romantic comedy must, at minimum, want its couple to be happy. This one seems unsure.

It's an animated picture about death, told from the point of view of a small bird, and it earns every ounce of the sentiment it asks for. The studio has clearly trusted its director, and the result is a film that takes risks most family animations would refuse to consider. I haven't cried in a cinema like that in years, and I left the theatre slightly stunned that this is the same studio responsible for last year's musical sequel.

The closing film of this year's festival is the rare end-of-week selection that actually deserves the slot. It is generous and accessible without being slight, the kind of picture that rewards a general audience while still containing enough beneath the surface to satisfy the critics who have sat through everything else. Sending an audience home moved rather than merely soothed is harder than it looks, and this film manages it.

The film has clearly spent its enormous budget on the world rather than the story, and the world is, to be fair, magnificent. The invented landscapes have a geographical coherence that fantasy cinema rarely bothers with, and the creatures feel like the products of an actual ecology. But two and a half hours into this gorgeously rendered place, I realised I did not care whether the prophecy was fulfilled, because the screenplay had given me a hero defined entirely by his destiny and not at all by his character.

The streaming film has been algorithmically assembled from the components of past successes, and watching it is like watching a survey of audience preferences rendered as drama. The premise tests well. The cast has been chosen for their separate fan bases. The runtime is calibrated to the platform's retention data. It is a competent, frictionless, entirely soulless product, and it will perform exactly as projected, and nobody will remember a frame of it a week later, which is, one suspects, fine by everyone who made it.

The film adapts a beloved fantasy novel, and the adaptation has been made by people who plainly love the book and have, in their love, forgotten that the audience has not read it. Characters arrive with the assumption that we already know them. Places are named as if their significance is established. The picture is dense with a reverence the uninitiated viewer cannot share, and the result is an epic that will delight its existing fans and bewilder everyone else.

The picture is a competent legal procedural that occasionally rises to something more. The procedural beats are reliable. The supporting cast is solid. What lifts it above its category is a single courtroom scene about two-thirds in, in which the defence lawyer, played with extraordinary unfussiness by an actor I had previously dismissed, refuses to cross-examine a witness. The refusal is dramatised at length. The rest of the film never quite reaches that altitude again, but a single moment of genuine craft is enough to recommend the picture.

The screenplay has clearly been worked over by a committee, and the seams show in every scene. There are jokes that belong to a raunchier film and jokes that belong to a sweeter one, and the tonal whiplash never settles. The two leads are doing their professional best, but they have been handed characters whose motivations change between scenes to suit whatever beat the plot requires next. The film is a reminder that the romantic comedy is one of the hardest forms to get right, and that good intentions are not enough.

The film's great achievement is its refusal of the redemption arc. The protagonist is a corrupt cop at the start and a corrupt cop at the end, and the screenplay does not flinch from the consequences of that constancy. What changes across the runtime is only how clearly he sees himself, and the picture treats that clarity as its own kind of punishment. It is a bleak, rigorous, beautifully acted film, and I cannot imagine it finding a wide audience, which is the genre's recurring tragedy.

What this survival picture understands is that the real drama begins after the disaster, not during it. The shipwreck is dispatched in the first ten minutes. The remaining ninety are spent on a raft, and the film has the courage to make those ninety minutes about the slow administrative horror of rationing, the small cruelties of exhaustion, the way a group of strangers negotiates who will be allowed to die first. It is a harrowing, intelligent film about the logistics of catastrophe.

The film follows a fictional regional planning committee through a season of internal disputes about the relocation of a small roundabout, and against any reasonable expectation the picture is genuinely funny for the full ninety minutes. The cast is uniformly excellent, and the screenplay's affection for the precise institutional language of local government is the rarest of comic gifts. The picture knows the difference between a motion and a resolution, and the difference, in the right hands, turns out to be a comic engine.

The signature long take is becoming a problem. It used to be a tool the director picked up when a scene demanded it; in the new film, it is the default setting, and a great many ordinary moments are being asked to bear weight they were never meant to carry. The picture is full of beautiful images and tired ideas, and one wishes someone in the editing room had been brave enough to suggest that perhaps not every conversation needs to be filmed in a single seven-minute setup.

The film opens with a five-minute heist that's wittier and more inventive than any of the dozen other heists I've watched this year. Sadly, that turns out to be the high point. The rest of the picture wanders into a brooding revenge plot that the actors don't seem to believe in, and the climax involves a helicopter for reasons that the screenplay never quite justifies but is suspiciously confident about.

Watched in the right frame of mind, with the right number of friends in the room, the new straight-to-streaming creature feature is a delight. The CGI is plainly cheap, the screenplay was written in what must have been a single afternoon, and the lead is doing the kind of work that suggests she would rather have been somewhere else. None of this matters. The film has a confident sense of its own pleasures, and within the small territory of those pleasures, it is funny and brisk and oddly satisfying.

Two hours of grey-on-grey digital sludge in search of a story. The set pieces have been edited within an inch of their lives, presumably to disguise the fact that the stunt team is doing most of the heavy lifting that the script declines to attempt. The lead has charisma to burn, which is just as well, because everyone around him is reciting exposition like they have a train to catch.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The picture arrives trailing two years of unhappy headlines, the firings, the budget overruns, the release date pushed three times, and the remarkable thing is how little of that chaos shows. Whoever finally took control of the edit has done heroic work, and the film, against every expectation, is coherent, controlled, and genuinely good. It is the rare troubled production that the audience would never guess was troubled at all.

The picture understands something most crime thrillers forget, which is that the most frightening character is rarely the one with the gun. The mid-level fixer at the centre of this film never raises his voice and never threatens anyone directly, and he is, by the final act, the most genuinely menacing screen presence I have encountered in years. The director films his ordinariness as horror. By the closing scene, an ordinary man eating breakfast has become almost unbearable to watch.

The disaster picture spends so long on the science of its impending catastrophe that the film forgets to be a film. There are lengthy scenes of experts pointing at screens, explaining the mechanics of the coming flood to one another and, transparently, to us. The screenplay has mistaken exposition for tension. When the flood finally arrives, it is almost a relief, not because the spectacle is thrilling but because the lecturing has finally stopped.

The constraints of the budget are visible in every frame, and the director has had the wisdom not to hide them. The film wears its poverty openly, and the openness becomes a kind of honesty, a refusal of the gloss that more expensive pictures use to flatter their audiences. It is a rough, immediate, deeply felt piece of work, and its roughness is not a flaw to be excused but a texture to be valued.

The time-travel logic in this film does not survive thirty seconds of conversation in the lobby afterwards, which is, I am told, traditional for the subgenre. What is more disappointing is that the picture does not seem to know its own logic doesn't hold, and the climactic emotional beat depends on a paradox the screenplay has already broken twice. The performances are committed, the score is propulsive, but the engine under the bonnet has been put together backwards.

I went in expecting another tasteful biopic and was caught off guard by how rude the film is willing to be about its subject. It refuses to canonise him. It refuses to redeem him. It lets the people he hurt say their piece without immediately balancing the books, and in doing so it tells you something true about the cost of a particular kind of public life. It's a serious, ungenerous, valuable film.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: The film opened on a handful of screens, received almost no advertising, and will be gone within the fortnight, and this is a small injustice, because it is one of the most quietly affecting pictures of the year. It has no stars, no hook, nothing a marketing department could seize on, only a beautifully written script and a cast of unknowns doing exceptional work. Seek it out before it vanishes.

I went in skeptical of yet another exorcism picture and was won over by about the twenty-minute mark. The film is unfashionably interested in the priest as a character rather than a vehicle, and his crisis of faith is more compelling than any of the spinning heads. The exorcism itself is staged with a restraint that today's audiences will not be used to. There are perhaps two effects in the whole final act, both perfectly placed and genuinely frightening.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The studio film has survived a production history that would have killed most pictures, and survival is the most that can be said for it. The thing is watchable. The thing is competent. But every choice on screen has the cautious, committee-sanded quality of a film that has passed through too many hands, and the result is a picture with no fingerprints on it, smoothed by its own troubled making into total anonymity.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The infamous production has finally yielded its film, and the film is, I am sorry to report, exactly as compromised as the headlines suggested. You can identify the original director's footage by its ambition and the studio's reshoots by their timidity, and the picture spends two hours visibly arguing with itself. Nobody won that argument. The audience, certainly, lost it.

It opens on a tracking shot through a rain-streaked kitchen window and never quite lets go of that mood. The film is interested in the shapes ordinary grief makes when it has nowhere public to go. The two leads, who could easily have lapsed into the awards-friendly gestures the role invites, instead play everything at a register just below speech. It's a small, exact film, and I'd take it over most of this year's noisier titles.

Three hours of digital battle in search of a story. The visual effects are some of the most expensive of the year and look it. The casualty count rises, the camera circles, the score swells, and absolutely nothing about any of it stays with me twenty minutes after I leave the cinema. War films at this scale used to be about something. This one is about being a war film, which is among the more depressing categories a film can fall into.

I appreciated the access. I appreciated the rare unguarded footage of a notoriously private subject. What I did not appreciate was the film's apparent allergy to any line of questioning that would have made him uncomfortable. The result is a documentary that feels less like journalism and more like a long, slightly sycophantic visit, and the gentle audience laughter at his self-deprecations only made the absence of harder questions louder.

The film is a throwback western that has decided, against all current fashion, to simply believe in the form. There is a clear hero, a clear villain, a town that needs saving, and a final showdown on a dusty street at noon. The picture executes these ancient shapes without irony and without apology, and the conviction is, after so many decades of revisionism, genuinely refreshing. Sometimes the old myths still have power, and this film trusts that power completely.

The home-front material is doing more work than the front-line material, which is the inverse of how this kind of picture usually breaks down. The director has found, in the wife's slow administrative grief over six months of telegrams and forms, a more cinematic subject than any of the explosions that occasionally interrupt it. The actress in the central role gives one of the year's best performances, and the film is wise enough to keep returning to her kitchen.

The picture casts the genre's iconography against itself with real intelligence. The lone rider arriving in town is, this time, a figure of menace rather than salvation; the saloon is a place of tedium rather than danger; the climactic duel is botched and ugly and over in a graceless instant. The film knows every convention it is inverting, and the inversions are precise rather than glib. It is the rare revisionist western that has actually thought about what it is revising.

The avant-garde has a long and honourable tradition of difficulty, but difficulty must be earned, and this picture mistakes opacity for rigour. The found footage is assembled without any discernible organising principle, the soundtrack is a wash of unmodulated noise, and the eighty-minute running time feels like a dare rather than a structure. There may be a film here that rewards the kind of attention I was unable to sustain. I suspect there is not, and the picture's defenders are responding to its reputation.

The score is the best thing in this otherwise unremarkable film, and it is doing so much narrative work that the picture would collapse without it. The composer has written a set of recurring themes that track the relationships between the characters with more precision than the screenplay manages, and there are emotional turns in the film that exist purely in the orchestration. It is a strange experience, watching a mediocre film carried almost entirely by its music, but the music is genuinely superb.

The animation is some of the most beautiful work the studio has ever produced. Backgrounds that look like watercolour breathing on the screen, character designs you want to cut out and keep in a notebook, a colour palette that changes with the protagonist's mood. The story is a little thin, and the score is overinsistent in the middle act, but as a piece of visual storytelling this is a small miracle.

The new restoration of this 1982 video-store cult favourite reveals a picture rather more thoughtfully made than its reputation suggested. The trim, eighty-minute runtime is the result of obvious cuts but also of unusually disciplined editing, and the kills are staged with a level of geographic clarity that more recent slashers have largely abandoned. The film was made for almost no money and looks it, but the craft within those constraints is real, and the restoration is a small act of cinematic justice.

The 1972 picture about a road trip down the Pacific coast is the most relaxed film in the director's career, and possibly his best. There is almost no plot. The performances feel improvised even when they are not. The score is a handful of period songs heard half-muffled through car windows. By the end of the picture, you feel as if you have travelled with these characters for a week, and you are sorry to see them get out of the car. It is a small miracle of a film.

The 1971 thriller arrives on the rep-house circuit looking like a different art form. There are no third-act explanations and no helpful flashbacks. The score is barely there. The lead, in the kind of role that would today be called showy, plays it with the bored exhaustion of a man who already knows how all of this is going to end. The film treats its audience as adults, and the absence of hand-holding feels like an entirely lost form of respect from a cinema we no longer have.

The film commits the cardinal sin of the sports genre, which is to make the actual sport boring. The matches are cut into incoherent fragments, the geography of the field is never established, and the audience is asked to feel the weight of a victory it could not actually follow. The off-field drama is fine. The performances are fine. But a sports film that cannot make its sport exciting has failed at the one task that distinguishes it from every other kind of film.

The film is hand-drawn at a level of detail that current studio economics should no longer make possible, and watching it you understand, scene by scene, where the budget actually went. A character's coat fluttering in a passing breeze contains the gestural information of a small performance in itself. The story is the studio's standard coming-of-age, more sweet than original, but the picture is a sustained argument for what the medium can still do when its makers refuse to compromise on the line.

Another handsome, airless costume drama in which everyone is too polite to say what they mean. The performances are uniformly distinguished, the lighting is uniformly soft, and the score is uniformly mournful. The film signals, every five minutes, that it would like to be considered intelligent and adult, but the political stakes it gestures towards are kept safely off-screen, and the central love story is paced like a careful museum walk. By the end I had been impressed and bored in roughly equal measure.

The first-time director has done something genuinely hard, which is to make a small film feel complete. There is no sense, watching this debut, of a filmmaker reaching beyond her means or padding a thin idea to feature length. The story is exactly the size of the running time. The visual style is exactly as elaborate as the material requires and no more. It is the work of someone who already understands the most difficult thing about directing, which is knowing what kind of film you are actually making.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: What this concert film understands is that the camera should serve the music rather than perform alongside it. The director keeps her shots long, lets the songs play out in something close to real time, and trusts that watching a great musician work is interesting enough without constant intervention. The result is the rare concert film that genuinely transports, and by the encore I had forgotten I was watching a screen rather than standing in the crowd.

What this picture understands is that the worst part of any haunting is the months before anything quite happens. The kitchen always feels slightly cooler than the hallway. The dog won't go up the stairs. Cups end up on the wrong shelf. The director lets all of this accumulate without ever underlining it, and by the time the actual entity appears, the house itself has already done most of the work. It is the most psychologically sophisticated horror I have seen this year.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: The film has divided critics, and the division falls along a fault line worth naming, which is the question of whether a picture's intentions can redeem its execution. The detractors say the execution is a mess. They are not wrong. The defenders say the intentions are visionary. They are not wrong either. I find myself, narrowly, with the defenders, because a glorious mess still has the glory in it.

The reboot has been engineered with the cold precision of a corporate relaunch. Every element of the beloved franchise has been polished, modernised, and made safe, and the resulting film has the texture of a product rather than a story. The new cast is attractive and capable. The effects are state of the art. And the whole enterprise is suffused with a focus-grouped caution that the scrappy original would not have recognised, because the original was made by people taking a risk, and this is made by people protecting an asset.

An indie shot on a microbudget that punches well above its means. The camera work is jittery in a way that initially feels accidental and later turns out to be a real aesthetic choice. The lead, who I'd not seen before, gives the kind of debut performance that should change his life. The story is a familiar coming-of-age, but it's told with such specificity of place and class that the familiarity stops mattering.

There is a particular poignancy in watching a great actress, late in life, in a role that is plainly about lateness itself. The part is a woman taking stock, and the performer brings to it the accumulated authority of fifty years of work, and the line between the character's reckoning and the actress's own becomes, by the final scene, impossible and unnecessary to draw. It is a magnificent farewell, if that is what it proves to be.

I admired the ambition and resented the execution. The film wants to be a sprawling crime epic in the mode of the genre's great urban tapestries, juggling a dozen characters across a corrupt city, but it has neither the running time nor the screenplay discipline to make the structure cohere. Threads are introduced and abandoned. Characters vanish for forty minutes and return as strangers. There is a genuinely great forty-minute film buried in this overstuffed two-and-a-half-hour one.

The casting of the lead has been the talk of the industry for a year, and on screen the experiment mostly works. The voice is not the operatic instrument the role traditionally requires, but the performance compensates with an interior dramatic life that previous interpreters have skipped over. The picture loses something in the soaring moments and gains something in the quiet ones, and on balance I would call the trade a net positive.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The picture's production was a disaster by every account, and the studio's decision to release it at all has the feel of cutting a loss rather than launching a film. Watching it, you sympathise. The movie is incoherent, the central performance was clearly assembled from incompatible takes, and the visual effects in the final act were plainly never finished. It is less a film than the archaeological remains of one.

The picture has been positioned, with some confidence, as the front-runner, and having seen it I find the confidence misplaced. The film is handsome and well-acted and utterly without surprise, a procession of the exact scenes the prestige drama is contractually required to provide. It will be nominated. It will probably win things. And it will be forgotten faster than the messier, braver films it is about to defeat.

By the third static long take of a man eating soup, I started to suspect this was less a film than a dare. The director is plainly talented, and there are individual frames here that belong in a gallery, but the picture mistakes austerity for rigour, and refuses to admit that any image, however composed, eventually has to mean something. Two hours of beautifully shot withholding is, in the end, withholding.

The film is a romantic comedy that has been edited as if it were a thriller, and the mismatch is exhausting. Scenes are cut short before their jokes can breathe, conversations are intercut for a tension the material does not contain, and the score keeps insisting on an urgency the gentle story does not want. Somewhere beneath the frantic assembly is a charming small film about two shy people. The editing has buried it, and I left wishing I could see the director's cut at half the speed.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: The film disappointed me on first viewing and astonished me on the second, and the gap between those two responses is the most interesting thing I can tell you about it. The picture demands that you already know its shape before you can see its detail, which is a real flaw in a marketplace that grants films one chance. But for the viewer willing to return, the reward is genuine, and the second viewing is a different and far better film.

There is a sequence at the centre of this espionage picture, a dead-drop exchange in a crowded railway station, that is staged with such precise control of information that I held my breath for its entire ten minutes. We know what the agent knows, we know what she does not, and we can see the danger she cannot, and the director orchestrates those gaps with the skill of a master. The rest of the film is merely good. That sequence is a small masterpiece of pure cinema tension.

The remake of a horror classic falls into the trap that swallows nearly all of them, which is the assumption that better technology means better horror. The original frightened audiences with suggestion, with what the cheap effects of its era could not afford to show. The new film can afford to show everything, and shows it, and the explicitness drains away every drop of dread. Fear lives in the imagination, and this remake has spent its entire budget on leaving nothing to imagine.

The film takes on a subject that most pictures would not dare to approach, and the courage of the attempt deserves acknowledgement before anything else. Whether the film handles the material responsibly is a separate and harder question, and my answer is a qualified yes. The director has resisted both sensationalism and false comfort, and the result is genuinely difficult to watch, which is, given the subject, exactly as it should be.

The compiled soundtrack of period pop songs is doing the film no favours. Each needle-drop is so on-the-nose, so literally illustrative of the scene it accompanies, that the picture begins to feel like an extended advertisement for its own album. The songs are good songs. But a soundtrack is not a playlist, and a film that deploys its music this lazily, as mood-by-association rather than as genuine scoring, has abdicated one of cinema's most powerful tools.

The documentary is shaped around a single, terrible interview with the subject's surviving sister, and once you've seen it, the whole tone of the film makes sense. Everything before that point is a careful clearing of the ground. Everything after is the slow, dignified work of refusing the obvious frame. It's the rare biographical documentary that lets you watch a filmmaker change her mind on screen, and the effect is enormously moving.

The streaming film arrives with the strange weightlessness of something that has skipped every traditional rite of release. There were no reviews embargoed for a premiere, no festival debut, no opening weekend. The picture simply appeared one Friday among forty other new titles, and it will disappear back into the catalogue within a fortnight. It is a perfectly decent film, and it has been denied any of the cultural occasion that would let an audience actually notice it, and that denial is its own quiet tragedy.

The film's gimmick — the heist takes place in real time, in a single ninety-minute shot, with no edits — is the kind of thing that should call attention to itself in a damaging way and somehow does not. The choreography of crew, security, cameras and incident is so precisely engineered that the single-take quality reads as urgency rather than virtuosity. The picture is a small miracle of preparation, and I suspect it will be studied by other filmmakers for a long time.
