Every fight is shot in close-up. Every chase is cut between three cameras. Every emotional beat is underlined by a wash of synths that arrived from a different film. By the time the credits roll, the eye is exhausted and the brain has been on autopilot for a full hour, and the only sensation I can name is the lingering ache of having sat in the same seat for too long.

The post-heist material is where this picture finally locates its real subject. The crew has succeeded. The money is in the bag. And then the film follows them, slowly, through six months of waiting in safehouses, growing apart, becoming suspicious of one another, and discovering that the success they had been working towards has not arrived in the form they expected. The picture is finally a film about the impossibility of going home after a victory, and it is the smarter for taking the long route to that question.

The film has been made for streaming, and it bears all the marks of the format's particular pathologies. It is too long, because length is now a metric of value, and it has been edited with the assumption that the viewer is doing something else, every plot point restated two or three times so that nobody glancing at their phone will lose the thread. There may be a tight ninety-minute film inside this bloated two-hour-twenty one, but the economics of streaming actively discourage anyone from finding it.

The festival's closing film arrived with the burden of ending the week on a note of significance, and the picture has been built, visibly, to carry that weight. It is earnest, it is timely, and it concludes with the kind of swelling uplift that a gala audience can applaud through tears. I distrusted the calculation even as it worked on me, and I left admiring the engineering more than the film.

The sports film is a genre of foregone conclusions, and this picture knows it, which is why it spends so little time on whether the team will win. The actual matches are dispatched briskly. The film's attention is on the locker room, the long bus journeys, the slow erosion of a coach's certainty across a losing season. By treating the sport as the setting rather than the subject, the picture earns an emotional weight the standard underdog narrative never reaches.

The director has clearly studied the great chamber dramas of the seventies, and the imitation is reverent to the point of paralysis. Every conversation is staged like an exhibit, every doorway lit like an oil painting, and yet the people inside the frames never quite come alive. There is craft here, certainly, but craft without a pulse is a museum, not a film, and after two hours I felt I had wandered around it dutifully and was ready to leave.

The colonial-administration backdrop is handled with more delicacy than I had expected. The film does not stage easy moral lessons in the bungalow, and the protagonist is allowed to remain compromised in the ways the era's letters and diaries record. The performance of the local clerk, played by an actor who is the best thing in nearly every scene, refuses every pity-prompt the screenplay puts in front of him, and the picture is enormously better for it.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: The film was made for very little money, released with even less fanfare, and is the kind of picture that critics are supposed to champion precisely because nobody else will. I am happy to do my part. It is a small, perfectly judged comedy-drama, and it deserves an audience far larger than the one the distributors have bothered to seek for it.

The film is a minor one, but it contains a major performance, and the performance comes from an actor most of the industry had quietly written off. He has been doing decorative work in undemanding films for a decade, and here, handed a real role at last, he reminds everyone what he can do. It is a late-career resurrection, and it is the kind of thing that should send casting directors back to their lists.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: There is a particular kind of good film that the current distribution system simply cannot accommodate, the modestly budgeted adult drama with no obvious selling point, and this picture is a textbook example. It is intelligent, well-acted, and genuinely moving, and it has been dumped into a few cinemas with no campaign behind it. It will be forgotten not because it is poor but because nobody was told it existed.

The film strands a single climber on a single mountain for its entire running time, and the constraint is the picture's making. There is almost no dialogue, because there is no one to talk to, and the drama is constructed entirely from the protagonist's diminishing options and the indifferent physics of cold and altitude. The lead carries the film alone, and she is more than equal to the task. It is a survival picture of genuine purity, a problem and a person and nothing else.

The picture is a fantasy adventure that has decided, refreshingly, to be funny. The quest is genuine and the stakes are real, but the screenplay never loses its sense of the inherent absurdity of prophecies and chosen ones, and the heroes are allowed to be irritated by the inconveniences of destiny. The humour does not undercut the wonder; it grounds it, makes the magic feel like something that happens to actual people. It is the most purely enjoyable fantasy film in years.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: There is an entire history of cinema's failure with child actors, the mugging, the cuteness, the sense of a small adult performing a script, and this film stands as a quiet rebuke to all of it. The director has clearly worked patiently with her young lead, drawing out a performance of total naturalness, and the picture's emotional power flows directly from that authenticity. It is a small family film, and it contains the best child performance I have seen in a decade.

The studio finally got the message: the audience wants this character, this director, and as little of the larger universe as possible. The result is a sequel that mostly behaves like a stand-alone. The supporting players from other films are kept to glimpses. The setting is closed off, the plot is contained, and the emotional arc is allowed to land without being interrupted by a setup for next summer's release. The picture is the better for the restraint, and the box office will, I suspect, reward the discipline.

The micro-budget film has a long history of punching above its weight, and this picture extends the tradition with real distinction. You can see the lack of money everywhere, in the handheld camera, the available-light photography, the locations that were obviously borrowed rather than built. None of it matters. The film has something far more valuable than money, which is a story worth telling and the conviction to tell it well.

There is a sequence in this picture, a slow push across a rain-soaked courtyard at dusk, that contains more genuine feeling than the entire screenplay. The cinematographer has understood the emotional content of the scene better than the writer did, and has built an image, the wet stone, the failing light, the single lit window, that carries the loneliness the dialogue keeps fumbling. It is a reminder that cinema is, finally, a visual medium, and that a great image can rescue a weak page.

The third-act problem is the most common failure mode in modern screenwriting, and this picture is a clinical example of it. The first hour establishes a complex web of relationships with real care. The final half-hour has to resolve that web, and it does so by simply cutting every knot at once, a flurry of confrontations and revelations and tidyings-up that no preceding scene had earned. The setup deserved a payoff. It got a cleanup.

Late-period work from this director tends to lean into the formal experiments earlier films only flirted with, and the new picture is the most extreme example yet. There are entire fifteen-minute stretches in which no character speaks, no action visibly advances, and yet the cumulative pressure on the viewer is enormous. I would not show this film to anyone unfamiliar with the rest of the work; for those who have come this far, it is a magnificent late statement.

The film commits to its mockumentary conceit with such patience that it occasionally forgets to be funny, and the picture is the better for it. The fake interviews accumulate weight rather than gags, the talking heads contradict each other in believable ways, and the central pseudo-investigation has the texture of a real local-news story rather than a comedy bit. The laughs, when they arrive, arrive almost as a release, and the picture's deepest pleasure is how seriously it takes its own nonsense.

There is a sequence in this disaster film, a slow flooding of a subway carriage, that is staged with such claustrophobic precision that I found it genuinely difficult to watch. The director understands that real terror is small and specific, the water at the ankles, then the knees, then the chest, the geometry of the carriage becoming a trap in real time. The rest of the picture is conventional spectacle. That one sequence is a small masterpiece of escalating dread.

The 1977 western, which I had remembered as a slightly minor entry in the director's filmography, is in fact one of his finest. The cinematography uses the desert as character rather than backdrop, and the lead performance is the kind of underplayed work that gives lesser actors permission to do less in similar parts ever after. The film is also notable for refusing to romanticise its violence, a discipline that would be largely abandoned within five years of its release.

The debut feature has all the marks of a filmmaker who has watched a great many films and not yet lived quite enough life to fill one. The picture is dense with stylistic flourishes, every one of them borrowed from a director the newcomer admires, and the borrowed gestures never settle into a voice of their own. There is undeniable craft here. What there is not, yet, is a reason for the film to exist beyond the maker's evident desire to make a film.

The film adapts the stage show with such reverence that it forgets to be a film. Every set looks like a set, every entrance is timed for an audience that isn't in the room, and every emotional climax is held a beat longer than the cinema can sustain. The original cast is doing its excellent work in the wrong medium, and the picture would, I suspect, play much better on a screen the size of a paperback than on the screen the size of a wall.

The opening twenty minutes in the trenches are an extraordinary piece of sustained filmmaking. The director keeps the camera at chest height and follows a single private through a rotation of duties, and by the time the first shell lands you have begun to understand the geography of the line in a way most war films never trouble to teach you. The rest of the picture cannot quite sustain that intensity, but the opening alone marks a genuine new arrival in the genre.

Another period coming-of-age picture set in a small town in the 1980s, this one differentiated principally by its willingness to be unhurried. There are entire reels in which almost nothing dramatic happens, and the picture instead trusts that the audience will enjoy spending time in this place with these people. The trust is well placed. The film's accumulated effect is greater than the sum of its scenes, which is the rare achievement, and the closing image is the kind that stays with you on the walk home.

The adventure is propelled by a quest so familiar that the audience can map its waypoints in advance, and yet the picture keeps finding small surprises in the execution. The wise mentor dies, as wise mentors do, but the film stays with the grief for an unfashionably long time. The dark lord is defeated, as dark lords are, but the victory is treated as a loss as much as a triumph. The shape is ancient. The texture of the telling is fresh enough to redeem it.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The famously difficult shoot has produced a famously difficult film, and the two facts are not unrelated. You can feel, watching it, the absence of a steady hand, the sense of a picture made by a production at war with itself. The performances vary wildly in register, as if the actors were each told a different story. It is a fascinating wreck, and I do not entirely regret the time spent picking through it.

A handsome, hollow crime picture that mistakes ambiguity for depth. The screenplay withholds information not because the withholding builds tension but because the writers seem unsure of the answers themselves. The lead investigator is given a tragic backstory delivered in fragments, none of which cohere into a person. The film ends on a freeze-frame that is plainly intended to haunt, and instead simply stops, leaving the audience to assemble a meaning the picture never bothered to provide.

The film is set on a Norfolk estate in the summer of 1912, and the production has clearly hired every consultant available. The horses are right, the watches are right, the buttonholes on the morning coats are right. What is not right is the screenplay, which has been written as a series of slow walks across lawns punctuated by significant looks. The looks are doing more dramatic work than the dialogue, which is a problem when the dialogue is supposed to be the engine of the picture.

Every beat of this boxing picture has been borrowed from a better boxing picture. The training montage arrives on schedule. The wise old trainer dispenses his wisdom. The protagonist loses the first big fight, retreats, rebuilds, and returns for the rematch. The fight choreography is competent and the lead has clearly trained hard, but the screenplay has nothing to offer that the genre has not already said a dozen times, and the film lands with the dull thud of an entirely predictable punch.

The festival's late-night sidebar continues to be the more interesting strand, and this entry — a chamber piece set in a single rural petrol station over the course of one rainy night — is the highlight of the section. The two leads are unknowns from the country's small theatre circuit, and they bring a register that no festival regular could have provided. The picture is small in every direction except the one that matters, which is what it asks the audience to feel.

The director, who has spent her last three films getting smaller and stranger, here gives us her most accessible work in a decade — which by her standards still means a two-hour-twelve-minute black-and-white feature about a translator's relationship with her dying mother. The compromises are real but never embarrassing. The picture is recognisably hers, and it is one of the warmer entries in a generally austere body of work. New viewers could reasonably start here.

The western has been beautifully photographed and indifferently written, and the imbalance is fatal. Every frame is a postcard, the desert rendered in colours of genuine splendour, and yet the people moving through this gorgeous country are stock figures reciting stock lines. The genre can survive a thin plot. It cannot survive characters this hollow, because the western has always been, at its best, a moral form, and a moral form requires people whose choices we can believe in.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: It will not trouble the box office, it will win no prizes, and within a month it will be a title in a streaming menu that nobody scrolls to, and all of this is a shame, because the film is lovely. It is a quiet picture about ordinary people, made with evident care, and its only crime is that it cannot be summarised in a sentence a marketer could use. Find it anyway.

There is a sequence midway through this epic, a long crossing of a frozen mountain pass, that achieves the genuine sublime. The director slows the picture almost to a halt, the score drops to a single sustained note, and the company of travellers becomes small dark figures against an overwhelming white expanse. For a few minutes the film stops being an adventure and becomes a meditation on human smallness, and the rest of the picture, good as it is, never quite reaches that altitude again.

The remake has done the genuinely difficult thing, which is to honour the original while disagreeing with it. The new film keeps the bones of the story but quietly reverses its sympathies, telling the same events from the side the original had cast as villains. It is a bold and respectful act of reinterpretation, and it sends you back to the original with fresh eyes. A remake this thoughtful is rare enough that I want to recommend the picture twice over.

It is a war film and a ghost story and a coming-of-age picture, all at once and without apology, and the combination should not cohere, and somehow it does. The director has understood that these three genres are all, at bottom, about the same thing, about how the past refuses to stay buried, and she has used that shared concern as the bridge between them. The film is strange and seamless, and I have seen nothing else like it.

The screenplay is doing a great deal of work to disguise the fact that it has no real character beneath the leader of the crew. Every other crew member is rendered through a single trait — the explosives one, the impulsive one, the woman who knew the inside person — and the picture lives or dies by whether the lead can carry the emotional weight of the group. He cannot quite. The actor is doing fine work, but the writing has handed him a chassis rather than a character, and the chassis is showing through.

What I admire about this picture is its willingness to be small. The first contact happens in a marsh, between two scientists and a creature that is mostly tentacle and patience. There are no fleet engagements, no government cover-ups, no Pentagon scenes. The drama is entirely about what the two of them are prepared to ask the creature and whether the creature is prepared to answer. By the end I had been moved by a science fiction film for the first time in years.

The picture handles its inflammatory subject with a restraint that some viewers will mistake for timidity, and they will be wrong. The restraint is the point. The director has understood that the loudest possible treatment of this material would also be the cheapest, and she has chosen instead a quiet, exact, deeply considered approach that respects the gravity of the subject far more than any sensational version could.

It is a war film built almost entirely out of waiting. The platoon arrives in the village, sets up the perimeter, and the picture stays with them through forty-eight hours of escalating apprehension that never quite breaks into action. Some audiences will find this maddening. I found it, by the closing minutes, almost unbearable in the right way. The director trusts that an audience will sit with anticipation if you give it real characters to anticipate alongside, and the trust pays off.

This is the film where the franchise officially runs out of ideas. There are perhaps two original sentences in the entire screenplay, and one of them is the title card. Every set piece is a slightly worse version of a set piece from one of the first three films, every character beat is a callback, and the cameos are now arriving so densely that the film loses the thread of its own plot to accommodate them. It is a museum tour pretending to be a movie.

The awards-season contender has been released in the prestige slot, late in the year, with the full apparatus of a campaign behind it, and the apparatus is louder than the film. The picture itself is a modest, decent drama that would, in spring, have been received as a modest, decent drama. Inflated to the dimensions of a front-runner, it cannot help but disappoint, and the disappointment is the campaign's fault, not the film's.

The robot in this film is the best non-human performance of the year, and most of that is sound and weight. The puppeteers have built a body that creaks and shifts as if it remembered being a different kind of machine. The voice work is doing the kind of subtle interior work the genre rarely allows. There are sequences in which the robot is alone in a room and the camera trusts that we will sit with it, and we do. I would watch a much longer cut of this film.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: The picture has been called a masterpiece and a disgrace in roughly equal measure, and the disagreement is not really about quality at all. It is about what the film is willing to do to its audience. The director has made a deliberately punishing work, and whether you regard the punishment as rigorous or sadistic is a question of temperament, not judgement. I found it rigorous. I came out shaken, and grateful to be.

The recently rediscovered cut of this 1978 picture is fifteen minutes longer than the original theatrical release, and almost all of the restored material is connective tissue rather than dramatic incident. It is, as a result, a better film by exactly the texture those fifteen minutes provide. The pacing of the original was already unfashionably slow; the longer version is slower still, and the picture begins to move in the way that a long evening moves, which is exactly the rhythm the story requires.

What the picture understands is that the funniest thing about a real documentary is rarely what the subject says but how they say it, and the imitation of that rhythm is where the comedy lives. The fictional retired conductor at the centre of this film delivers his anecdotes in exactly the cadence of a man who has been telling these stories at dinner parties for forty years. The picture's comedy is at the level of breath, not punchline, and is the better for it.

The film is based on a true story, and it has been crushed flat by its fidelity to the facts. Every scene has the dutiful quality of a screenplay ticking off events that really happened, and the picture never finds the dramatic shape that would have made those events feel inevitable rather than merely chronological. The sport is shot well enough. The people playing it remain strangers. A true story is not the same thing as a story, and this film never closes the gap.

There is a structural law that the third act must deliver on the promises of the first, and this film breaks the law spectacularly. The promises made in the opening act are subtle and human; the third act delivers, instead, a series of loud incidents that answer questions nobody was asking. It is as though two different screenwriters worked on the picture and never met, and the one who wrote the ending had not read the beginning.

It is the kind of film only this director could have made, and it has all the strengths and limits of that fact. The sensibility is unmistakable from the first shot. The themes are the ones he has been working on since his first picture. The collaborators are the same — his cinematographer of twenty years, his composer of fifteen — and the result is a film that is both deeply familiar and, in its specifics, freshly painful in a way none of the previous work quite was.

It is the rare sequel that gives its returning star something honest to do. The character we have followed across four films is older, slower, and more compromised, and the picture stays inside that condition rather than pretending it can be papered over with a new haircut and a younger sidekick. The action is fewer and shorter than in any previous instalment. The emotional payoffs are the largest. It is a sad, satisfying film, and probably the right way to leave this story.

What distinguishes this film visually is its commitment to the static frame. The camera almost never moves. Scene after scene is composed as a fixed tableau, and the viewer's eye is left to travel within the image rather than being led around it by the director. It is an old-fashioned discipline, and it asks more of the audience than the modern restless camera does, but the rewards are real. Every frame here has been genuinely composed, and composition, properly done, is its own kind of storytelling.

The action choreography is genuinely thrilling — staged in long, legible takes that respect both the geography of the room and the physicality of the actors. The plot is the usual nonsense about a stolen device and a shadowy agency, but nobody in the cinema is here for the plot, and the film knows it. What it offers instead is a parade of properly thought-through set pieces, including a corridor fight that I will be replaying in my head for weeks.

After two decades of being celebrated for his stylistic restraint, the director has finally made a film that loosens up, and the change is welcome. The new picture has jokes. It has a genuinely warm supporting cast. It even, for the first time in his career, ends on a clearly hopeful image. Some critics will find the shift uncomfortable. I found it, after fifteen films of magnificent gloom, a kind of relief I did not realise I had been waiting for.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: I disliked this film the first time I saw it, and I have to report that a second viewing has substantially revised my judgement. What I took for slackness turns out to be patience, and what I took for obscurity turns out to be a structure that only reveals itself once you know where it is going. The picture rewards the return trip, and I now suspect my first response said more about my expectations than about the film.

The new midnight-movie release exists primarily to be watched at midnight by an audience that is partly drunk and entirely committed. It will play badly in any other setting. Within its setting, it is perfectly judged. The dialogue is engineered for the room to shout back at. The set pieces are arranged at the intervals at which a midnight audience would start to lose attention. The picture is not so much a film as a small social occasion, and judged as such it is one of the year's successes.

The aliens, when they finally arrive, look like every other set of aliens we have been shown since the early nineties. The picture trades on the sober first-contact mood that one or two recent films have established, but it has none of their patience or their ideas. The linguist protagonist solves the language puzzle off-screen, which is the wrong choice in a film whose entire premise is the puzzle. By the time the spacecraft lift off, I had stopped caring why they had come.

What this film understands is that the most interesting part of a sporting career is the ending. The protagonist is a footballer two years past his prime, and the picture is a clear-eyed study of a man whose body has begun to refuse the only thing it was ever celebrated for. There is no triumphant final match. There is a quiet, devastating series of smaller defeats, and a performance from the lead that finds the precise texture of an athlete learning to be ordinary.

For two and a half hours the film promises a reckoning it never delivers. There are immaculate compositions, a restrained score, and the kind of weighty silences that prestige cinema teaches us to mistake for depth, but the script ducks every difficult choice it sets up. The lead is doing real work in a part the screenplay refuses to meet halfway, and the result is a handsome, expensive shrug.

The biopic problem strikes again. The film hits the bullet points of its subject's life with a kind of dutiful efficiency, like a museum audio guide that's been told to keep moving. The actor in the lead role is doing fine work, occasionally great work, but the screenplay refuses to let him sit inside a single moment for long enough to be more than a series of impersonations. By the end I knew the chronology and not the person.

Returning to this picture in middle age, what surprised me is how funny it is. The reputation has hardened into a kind of weighty hindsight reverence, but the 1976 release was, scene by scene, a comedy first. The political darkness is real, but it is the absurdity of meetings and motel rooms and provincial diners that the film actually lives in. Comedy ages badly more often than not, and the laughs in this one have aged extraordinarily well.

Nothing in the film is wrong, exactly. The pacing is fine. The acting is fine. The action is fine. And yet nothing in the film is alive, either. It's been engineered by a focus group, photographed by a competent cinematographer, and scored by a composer who has clearly been instructed not to be memorable, and the result is the cinematic equivalent of beige carpet.

There is a sequence at the centre of this picture, in chambers with the judge, that may be the best three minutes of legal drama in the last decade. The two senior counsel and the bench find themselves in an off-the-record conversation about how a difficult ruling will be presented, and the picture, normally so committed to the public theatre of the courtroom, allows itself a sudden glimpse of the private craft beneath it. The film never quite recovers its energy afterwards, but that one scene justifies its existence.

The film is structured as a relay, each character handing the narrative to the next as their paths intersect across a single city over a single day. It is a clever conceit, and it sustains itself for about an hour before the cleverness begins to feel like a constraint. The handoffs grow contrived, the coincidences strain, and the picture becomes a demonstration of a structural idea rather than a story. The ensemble deserved a looser frame, and the frame slowly suffocates them.

There is a sequence in this debut, a single unbroken shot following the protagonist through a crowded house party, that announces the arrival of a real filmmaker more clearly than any amount of advance press. The choreography of camera and crowd and incident is the work of someone with a genuine spatial imagination. The rest of the film does not always live up to that sequence, but a debut only needs to contain one moment of undeniable command, and this one contains several.

Three sequels in, the franchise has settled into a comforting rhythm that I find I no longer resent. The pleasures are modest and well-judged. The lead is doing slightly more interior work than the role requires. The supporting cast is given dignified material instead of comic-relief slop. The villain is, for once, given an actual argument rather than a costume. None of this is going to win prizes, and none of it is trying to. It is, simply, a good Wednesday-night cinema trip.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The picture is a hagiography in concert-film clothing. The artist at its centre is presented without a single moment of friction or doubt, the interviews are uniformly adoring, and the film has the suspiciously frictionless texture of a project made with the subject's full cooperation and full editorial control. The performance footage is good. The portrait around it is so flattering as to be useless, and the audience leaves having been sold something rather than shown anything.

The picture is one of those holiday-gathering ensemble dramas in which an extended family convenes under one roof and the old wounds are reopened over the course of a long weekend. The form is familiar, but the film executes it with unusual honesty. Nobody is redeemed by the closing scene. The reconciliations are partial and provisional, the way real family reconciliations are, and the ensemble is good enough to make every grudge and every grudging truce feel earned.

The thriller is structured as a single long night, and the constraint serves it well. The detective moves from one location to the next as the city empties out around her, and the picture accumulates a kind of fatigue that mirrors her own. The dialogue is sharp without being showy. The eventual resolution is smaller than the genre usually permits, a matter of a confession given quietly in a diner at dawn, and the modesty of that ending is precisely what makes it land.

The picture wants to deconstruct the western and ends up merely decorating it. The screenplay gestures at the genre's complicity in the mythology of conquest, has its characters deliver the occasional speech of self-aware critique, and then proceeds to stage exactly the kind of thrilling gun battle the critique was supposedly dismantling. You cannot have it both ways. A film that wants to interrogate the western's pleasures cannot also serve them up undiminished, and this one tries, and the contradiction hollows it out.

I laughed harder than I have at any cinema release this year. The screenplay is dense in the best way — there are jokes underneath jokes, three actors all riffing at the top of their game, and a willingness to let a scene end on a beat that nobody saw coming. It's also, almost incidentally, the most warm-hearted comedy in a decade. Take everyone you know who has been having a hard week.

The conventional reading of this 1970 debut — that it is technically rough and morally ambitious — has hardened into something close to received wisdom, and the new restoration is worth seeing precisely because it pushes back against that reading. The picture is, in fact, technically more accomplished than its reputation suggests. The hand-held camera work is purposive rather than accidental. The framing of the long courtroom scene is the work of a confident filmmaker, not a fledgling. The picture has been undersold by its own legend for fifty years.

The actor is well into his seventies now, and the performance he gives here is the finest of his long career, which is not a sentence one writes often. Age has stripped away every trace of technique, every actorly flourish, and what remains is something close to pure presence. He does almost nothing, and the almost-nothing is devastating, and the film is wise enough to simply point the camera at him and wait.

The dialogue scenes between songs are doing the work, in this picture, that the songs themselves cannot. The numbers are professional and forgettable; the conversations are excellent. There is a kitchen-table argument in the second act, sung by two characters who are very tired and very fond of each other, that is the best moment in the film, and it is not really a musical moment at all but a piece of dialogue that has, with great care, been set to a half-melody behind it.

The film assembles a dozen significant characters and, against all odds, gives each of them a genuine interior life. The screenplay's structural achievement is that no thread feels like filler, no character feels like a device, and the cross-cutting between stories generates meaning rather than mere momentum. The ensemble is uniformly excellent, but the real star is the editing, which knows precisely when to leave one story and which fragment of another to land on. It is a master class in choreographing a crowd.

The picture is unusual among modern spy films in being genuinely interested in the moral cost of the work. The protagonist is good at his job, and the film makes us understand that being good at this particular job means betraying people who trusted him, repeatedly, as a matter of routine professional competence. There is no glamour here. The screenplay treats each betrayal as a small wound to the man's character, and by the final scene the accumulated damage is visible on his face.

The closing-night picture is a film about filmmaking, which is the safest possible choice for a room full of people who make films, and the audience responded to its flattering portrait of their profession exactly as the programmers must have hoped. I confess I am tired of cinema's endless self-regard. The picture is well-made, and its subject is the one subject a festival audience can be relied upon to find irresistible.

What this picture grasps, and most of its peers do not, is that the comedy and the romance have to be the same thing. The jokes are not decorations hung on the love story; they emerge from the specific friction between two people who are wrong for each other in interesting ways. The screenplay is dense with the kind of dialogue that rewards attention, and the leads deliver it at the brisk pace the form demands. It is the funniest and the most genuinely romantic film I have seen all year.

It's a documentary about a small-town swimming coach, and it has no business being as gripping as it is. The director has the patience to let the coach contradict himself across the years of footage, and the editing is rigorous in a way that respects both the man and the people he disappointed. By the closing minutes, the film has earned a complexity that bigger, splashier documentaries about more famous lives never come close to.

The small-budget film is often praised in a slightly condescending register, as a brave little effort, and I want to avoid that register entirely, because this picture deserves better than condescension. It is one of the three or four best films I have seen this year, and its budget is a piece of trivia, not an excuse. The triumph here is not that they made a film cheaply. The triumph is that they made a film this good.

The trial occupies the middle two hours of the film and is the most engrossing courtroom drama in a generation. The director resists the temptation to cut away to flashbacks and instead trusts that the testimony itself — careful, slow, contradictory — will be the dramatic material. The judge is played with magnificent neutrality. The witnesses come and go with the unforced texture of real witnesses. By the time the verdict arrives, we have lived through the trial alongside the jury, and the verdict is unbearable in exactly the right way.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The concert film is shot across three nights of the same tour, and the director has cut between them with such skill that the seams are invisible, assembling an idealised single performance from the best moments of each. Purists may object to the artifice. I found it exhilarating. The film is not a document of one night but a portrait of what the band was capable of on its best night, and the editing's quiet construction of that ideal is itself a kind of love letter to the music.

A slasher dressed in awards-season clothing. The film thinks that slow camera moves and a desaturated palette excuse the fact that its kills are perfunctory and its characters interchangeable. The killer's mask is a striking object and will sell some merchandise. The film around the mask is a series of corridor chases interspersed with monologues about trauma that the screenplay has not earned. It is dressed up so seriously you'd think it had something to say.

The epic runs to nearly three hours, and for the first two of them I was wholly under its spell. The world-building is generous, the performances are committed, and the central journey has a real momentum. Then the film reaches its enormous final battle, and the picture seems to lose all confidence in the human story it had been telling, drowning its characters in an hour of indistinguishable digital carnage. A great film is in here, and it ends, in my estimation, around the two-hour mark.

Shot on grainy 16mm and dubbed in a style that draws attention to its own artifice, this is the kind of indie that wears its references as a kind of armour. The dialogue is so painfully arch you can hear the screenwriter laughing in the margins, and the performances are pitched at the same key throughout, somewhere between bored and wounded. There's a film struggling to be itself in here, but the affectation suffocates it.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: You can see the trouble on screen, frame by frame. The film was famously reshot, recut, and handed to a second director, and the seams of all that interference are visible in every reel, scenes that belong to different films, a tone that lurches, a third act that has plainly been assembled from whatever footage survived. There is a real picture buried in here somewhere, and the production has comprehensively destroyed any chance of finding it.

The fantasy adventure has become a genre of exhausting completeness, every corner of its world explained, every magical rule codified, every culture given its appendix of lore. This picture is a quiet rebellion against that tendency. Its magic is genuinely mysterious, never fully accounted for, and the film is the more enchanting for its restraint. The protagonist does not understand the forces she is moving among, and neither do we, and that shared bewilderment is the source of real wonder.

It's the eighth film in the series and the formula is showing its seams. We get the new gadget, the obligatory rooftop chase, the betrayal from a familiar face, and a closing one-liner that lands with an audible thud. The lead is still magnetic, the practical effects team is still doing fine work, but the writing has settled into a shape that's content to copy itself rather than risk anything new.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: On first viewing the ending struck me as a cheat, and I left the cinema annoyed. On second viewing, knowing what was coming, I watched the film lay its groundwork with absolute scrupulousness, and the ending now strikes me as inevitable rather than arbitrary. The picture did not change. My ability to see what it was doing changed, and that is the particular gift of a film that improves on return.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The picture is a music documentary that has confused access with insight. The filmmakers were granted extraordinary proximity to the artist, and the screen is full of intimate footage, backstage, on the bus, in hotel rooms. But proximity alone reveals nothing, and the film never finds an angle, a question, an argument about its subject. It simply follows him around for two hours, and at the end we have been very close to a person we have not, in any meaningful sense, come to know.

The closing number of this picture is one of the longest in any musical I can remember, running close to twelve uninterrupted minutes, and the director has staged it with such structural cunning that I never once checked my watch. Choreographic ideas accumulate, then recombine, then recede; the lyric carries forward without ever repeating itself; and the camera knows exactly when to come in close and when to step back. It is the rare ending that earns its scale.

The film is the kind of melancholy anime feature that has become the international face of the form: small towns, summer evenings, characters separated by impossibly arranged circumstances, and trains arriving at platforms a few seconds too late. There is nothing exactly original in the assembly. There is, however, real craft in the specifics — a particular cicada sound under a particular rooftop scene, a particular shade of late-afternoon light through a particular train window — and the picture earns its sentiment.

The picture is set across a single summer in a coastal town and it has the rare gift of treating its teenagers as actual people rather than vehicles for nostalgia. The screenplay refuses to be sentimental about the period the filmmaker is plainly remembering. The friendships are awkward, the romance is partial, the older relatives are neither saintly nor monstrous, and the ending is small and quiet in the way real summers actually end. It is one of the year's most affecting films.

There is a fundamental dishonesty to this thriller that soured me on it well before the end. The film withholds a crucial piece of information not from the characters but from the audience alone, and it does so by actively misrepresenting what we are shown. The eventual reveal therefore does not reframe the story; it simply admits that the picture lied to us. A psychological thriller can keep secrets. It cannot cheat, and this one cheats, and the cheating undoes everything that came before.

There is a long and honourable tradition of films that refuse to sit in a single genre, and there is also a tradition of films that mistake genre confusion for genre transcendence, and this picture, regrettably, belongs to the second. It lurches between thriller, romance, and satire without ever committing to any of them, and the result is not a hybrid but a muddle, a film that has avoided every genre's discipline and inherited none of their strengths.

I expected a competent superhero picture and got something closer to a war film with a cape. The director treats the destruction with weight, not delight, and the lead is asked to play exhaustion as well as heroism. It overstays by twenty minutes and the climactic battle is a step backwards into the genre's worst habits, but for most of its runtime this is the best film of its kind in years.

It is the rare debut that arrives fully formed, and this one mostly does. The young director has a confident visual sense and an even more impressive sense of restraint, knowing exactly when to hold a shot and when to cut away. There are first-feature wobbles, a slightly overwritten voiceover, a third act that resolves a beat too neatly, but they are the wobbles of genuine talent. This is a filmmaker worth following, and the picture is a real arrival.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The newly restored print of this 1924 feature is a revelation, and not only for the obvious technical reasons. Freed of the murk that decades of bad prints had imposed, the film's astonishing visual storytelling finally registers. There is a chase sequence across a moving train that is as legible and as thrilling as anything in modern action cinema, accomplished entirely through composition and cutting. We have spent a century underrating this director, and the restoration is a quiet correction.

Watching the new film with the previous six in mind, you begin to see how completely this director has been making the same movie since 1998, and how patient and various the variations have been. The recurring obsessions — interrupted phone calls, hands held at the wrong angle, weather that arrives a scene too early — are now so embedded in the work that they have become a private grammar. The new picture is one of the finer entries in the cycle, and I suspect it is a late one.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: There is a category of film that is built to be seen twice, and this is one of them, though it does not announce the fact. The first viewing is a slightly bewildering experience of withheld information. The second is something close to revelation, every early scene now legible, every apparently throwaway detail revealed as load-bearing. It is a genuine feat of construction, and it asks, not unreasonably, for your patience and your second ticket.

There is a particular pleasure in a coming-of-age film that respects its grown-ups. The parents in this picture are not obstacles; they are people, with their own ongoing private failures, and the screenplay allows them to be wrong about specific things and right about others. The teenager at the centre is therefore growing up in a real ecology rather than against a cardboard cutout, and the picture's accumulated emotional weight is the result of that demographic honesty.

Animated for children, plotted for tired parents, scored for nobody in particular. The studio's house style has now flattened into a kind of high-gloss interchangeability, where every protagonist has the same haircut and every villain is voiced by the same British comedian, and you can predict each beat to the second. The film is harmless, professionally made, and entirely forgettable, which is the worst thing you can say about a film made for children.

The picture takes place almost entirely inside a single character's recovering memory, and the unreliability is structural rather than decorative. Scenes are replayed with small differences, conversations shift their meaning on the second hearing, and the audience is asked to assemble the truth from a set of contradictory drafts. It is a demanding film, and it does not flatter the viewer with a tidy final version of events. The refusal is the point, and it is a brave one in a genre addicted to closure.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The concert film captures a single legendary night, and the director has wisely resisted the temptation to dress it up. There is no narration, no interview material, no context beyond the performance itself. The picture simply presents the show, song by song, from the soundcheck to the final bow, and the absence of editorial intervention is what makes it work. We are given the night, whole, and asked to make of it what we will, and what I made of it was something close to elation.

The picture refuses every genre it flirts with, and the refusal is exhilarating. Each time you think you have identified what kind of film this is, what kind of ending it must be building toward, it slips the category and becomes something else, and the experience of watching it is one of continuous productive disorientation. It will frustrate viewers who want to know where they stand. It rewarded me precisely because it never let me know.

A sweet, modest comedy that knows exactly what kind of film it wants to be and gets out before the welcome wears off. Both leads are gifted physical comedians, and the director has the rare confidence to let them work in long takes, which is increasingly unusual in modern comedy. The jokes are not all gold, but enough of them land, and the film has a final scene of unexpected emotional weight.

The picture is the kind of all-star disaster movie the genre produced in bulk decades ago, and the revival is not as fun as the filmmakers plainly hoped. The famous faces are introduced in their familiar archetypes, the catastrophe arrives on schedule, and the audience settles in to guess the order of the deaths. The effects are expensive and the pace is brisk, but the film never finds the cheerful self-awareness that made the genre's classics enjoyable. It takes its own silliness far too seriously.

The trouble with the heist genre at the moment is that the screenplays have started to mistake complication for plotting. This picture is a case study. There are seven separate twists, four interlocking double-crosses, and at least two extra plans concealed beneath the surface plan, and the cumulative effect is exhausting rather than thrilling. The actors are doing their best to keep up. The audience, somewhere around the fifth reveal, simply gives up trying to track what was a misdirection in the first place.

It's a quiet shaggy-dog comedy that builds its laughs out of a sustained refusal to escalate. Nobody shouts, nobody chases anyone through traffic, and the central joke — a long-running argument about a wedding venue — keeps quietly mutating in the background of every scene. Both leads play their roles slightly past the point of irritation, which is a hard register to maintain, and the picture earns its small ending by trusting that the audience has been paying attention all along.

What lingers is the central performance. The actress holds the film at the point where dignity becomes brittleness, and from that point onward you watch her choose, breath by breath, between staying upright and finally giving up. The script around her is sometimes too tidy in its symmetries, but her work is so honest that the architecture stops mattering. This is the best lead performance of the year, in any genre.

What a pleasure to find a musical that lets its supporting cast sing. The leads do their leading-cast work, but the show really belongs to the chorus, who are given two genuinely virtuosic group numbers that the camera mostly keeps wide enough to appreciate. The film has the warmth of an actual stage company that has been working together for months, which in the era of pre-recorded vocals and individual cubicles is not a small accomplishment.

The picture's first half is one of the most sustained comic performances of the year. The fictional management consultant at its centre is so precisely observed — the half-coherent jargon, the conference-circuit anecdotes, the watch worn slightly too loosely — that I had to keep reminding myself this was not a real person. The second half loses some of its discipline as the screenplay reaches for an emotional arc the form does not quite support, but the first half alone is worth seeing.

The animated documentary, an awkward category, finds in this picture one of its strongest examples. The subject is a Cold War defector whose story can no longer be verified in primary archives, and the director has elected to render the disputed sequences in drawn animation rather than dramatised reconstruction. The decision is morally serious and visually striking. The film never pretends to be showing us the past; it is showing us what the past sounds like in the testimony of a man who is no longer sure of his own memory.

For two acts this is an exceptional film, and I want that on the record before I describe what goes wrong, because for two acts it is genuinely exceptional. The characters are rich, the situation is gripping, the direction is assured. And then the third act arrives, and the picture, as if seized by panic, abandons everything it had built in favour of a frantic mechanical resolution that belongs to a much worse film.

What this documentary understands, and most don't, is that an archive is also a kind of authored text. The filmmakers have not just hoovered up footage; they've thought about what each clip was originally trying to say, and how to make a frame the original photographer never intended argue with itself. The result is a portrait of a public figure that feels genuinely contested rather than tidied up for the streaming algorithm.

The composer has written a score of genuine thematic intelligence, and the film's editors have, regrettably, chopped it to pieces. You can hear, in fragments, the shape of the music the composer intended, melodic lines that begin and are cut off, developments that are interrupted by a scene change. The score deserved a film cut to accommodate it. Instead it has been treated as wallpaper, trimmed to fit, and a fine piece of musical writing has been reduced to a series of stings.

The first feature from a director worth following. It's set inside the disordered apartment of a translator who has stopped leaving the house, and the film extracts something close to a thriller out of his attempts to finish a single sentence. The visual ideas are funny and specific, the performance is calibrated to the millimetre, and the picture knows exactly when to end, which is a rare instinct.

The digital effects in this fantasy epic have reached the point of total photorealism, and the picture is, paradoxically, the worse for it. When the dragons were puppets and the armies were extras, the eye registered a physical reality. Now everything is equally weightless and equally possible, and the spectacle no longer means anything because nothing in it could ever have failed. The film is a flawless rendering of events that never, in any sense, happened, and the flawlessness is its central emptiness.

The film centres on a public-defender's tribunal appearance that turns, halfway through, into the most engrossing professional collapse I have seen on film since the seventies. The actress in the central role does extraordinary, almost archeological work, peeling back layer after layer of professional polish until what is left at the lectern is recognisable but not yet broken. The screenplay refuses to forgive her at the end, which is the only honest choice. I will be thinking about this performance for a long time.

The revisionist western has been revising the same handful of myths for fifty years now, and this picture has nothing fresh to add to the conversation. We get the brutal demystification of frontier violence, the morally compromised lawman, the unromantic mud and disease, and all of it has been done before and done better. The cinematography is genuinely beautiful, all vast skies and small figures. But beauty is not an argument, and the film has no argument the genre has not already exhausted.

The debut is plainly autobiographical, drawn from the director's own childhood in a particular industrial town, and the specificity is the picture's great strength and its eventual limitation. The detail is exact and the affection is genuine, and for an hour the film is a vivid act of remembering. But memory is not yet structure, and the picture's final third drifts, accumulating incident without shape, as if the director could not bear to leave anything out. The next film, freed of the autobiography, may be the real one.

What is interesting about the new film is how visibly the director is wrestling with his own back catalogue. The recurring imagery is still here — the static of an empty channel, the half-eaten breakfast, the road photographed from a moving car — but the film is uneasy with these inheritances, and at several points seems to be actively arguing with the version of the director who made the earlier work. The argument is not always coherent. It is, however, the most alive he has seemed on screen in years.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The film keeps the play's real-time structure, ninety minutes of story told across ninety minutes of screen time, and the constraint gives the picture a relentless forward pressure. The director has resisted the urge to fragment the timeline, and the audience experiences the central confrontation at exactly the pace the characters do. It is an unfashionable kind of filmmaking, patient and confined, and it is also, by the final scene, almost unbearably tense. The stage origins are an asset, not a limitation.

The closing selection is a documentary, which is itself an unusual and welcome choice for a gala slot, and the film honours the decision by being genuinely stirring. It is the kind of non-fiction picture that builds, across two hours, toward an emotional release that an audience can share collectively, and the standing ovation at the end felt, for once, like a real response rather than a festival courtesy.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: There is a twist near the end of this film, and twist pictures are usually one-time experiences, the second viewing reduced to spotting the clues. This one is different. Knowing the twist does not exhaust the film; it deepens it, because the twist recontextualises every relationship rather than merely the plot, and the second viewing becomes an experience of watching characters who do not yet know what we now know. It is richer the second time, not poorer.

What distinguishes this prestige contender from the season's other strivers is that it seems genuinely unaware of its own awards potential. It is a serious film about a serious subject, and yet it never strikes the calculated poses, never pauses for the speech that exists to be clipped into a ceremony reel. The seriousness is real rather than performed, and that authenticity, in this season of campaigns, is itself remarkable.

The bridge sequence is the best thing this director has ever filmed. For seven uninterrupted minutes you understand exactly where every character is in space, what they want, and what's about to go wrong, and the rhythm of cuts and held shots is so confidently calibrated that you forget to breathe. The rest of the film never quite reaches that altitude again, but a single masterful sequence is reason enough to see it.

Festival catnip in the worst sense. The film checks every box the international competition slate currently rewards — austerity of style, marginalised protagonist, ambiguous ending, running time over two hours — and yet the assembly never adds up to a film with a felt centre. The director has clearly read the rubric. The picture is the answer to the question of how to win prizes, not the question of what a story is. By the second hour I was admiring the strategy and feeling nothing.

The film about a teenage migration across two countries is the rare coming-of-age picture that does not allow the political background to function as scenery. The young protagonist's awakening is inseparable from the geopolitical context, and the screenplay refuses to lift one out of the other for dramatic convenience. The film is intermittently brutal and consistently humane. The actress in the central role is going to win things, and she will deserve to.

The voice cast is doing wonderful work, but the screenplay has the structural integrity of damp cardboard. The picture lurches from one set piece to the next without ever explaining why we should care about the central friendship, and the third act resolves on a moral lesson so abrupt that I half-expected a teacher to walk out and turn on the lights. There are flashes of inventive animation, but they're stranded in a film that doesn't know what it wants to say.

The Vietnam picture in this director's hands is unexpectedly intimate. There are no command-tent scenes, no helicopter overshots, no maps with red arrows. There is one platoon, one valley, one week, and the cumulative attrition of decisions made by men who can no longer remember the larger argument they are supposedly part of. The picture is built out of small, accurate moments — a letter, a meal, a misunderstanding — and it left me shaken in ways the larger Vietnam canon rarely manages.

What moves me about this late-career performance is its lack of vanity. The actress has allowed herself to be filmed as the age she actually is, allowed the role to be about diminishment, allowed her character to be tired and frightened and small. A performer this celebrated has every incentive to protect her image, and she has refused to, and the refusal is itself a kind of artistic courage that the film is fortunate to contain.

There is a particular pleasure in watching a film that has clearly had to be clever about its poverty. This picture is set almost entirely in a single house, has a cast of four, and unfolds across one night, and every one of those limitations was plainly a budgetary necessity that the screenplay has transformed into a virtue. The confinement is the tension. The smallness is the intimacy. It is a triumph of resourcefulness.

The CGI feature studios have learned to make these films interchangeable, and this one is interchangeable in all the predicted ways. The lead is voiced by the comedian whose voice the studio is currently leasing. The sidekick is the small mammal whose toy line is currently being tested. The villain is a comically over-elaborate corporate executive. The animation itself is technically excellent and aesthetically void, and the cinema, when I attended on Saturday afternoon, was full of children who appeared to be enjoying themselves anyway.
